source_text: Ecce idem Moyses refert alio in loco, quod Abrahae uisus sit deus. quod nemo hominum deum uideat et utuat. potest deus, quomodo uisus est deus? quomodo uideri non potest? inquit, wdit umguam; hominum nemo, nec uidere potest. mentitur; ergo uere uisus est deus. ex quo intellegi potest, quod non pater uisus sit, qui numquam uisus est, sed filius, qui et descendere solitus est, et uideri quia descenderit. imago ro est enim éinuisibilis dei, ut mediocritas et fragilitas condicionis humanae deum patrem uidere aliquando iam tunc assuesceret in imagine dei, hoc est, in filio dei. gradatim enim et per incrementa fragilitas humana nutriri debuit per imaginem ad istam gloriam, ut deum patrem uidere possit aliquando, periculosa sunt enim quae magna sunt, si repentina sunt. nam etiam lux solis subita post tenebras splendore nimio insuetis oculis non ostendet diem, sed potius faciet caecitatem. quod ne in damnum humanorum contingat oculorum, paulatim disruptis et dissipatis tenebris, ortus luminaris istius mediocribus incrementis fallenter assurgens oculos hominum sensim assuefacit ad totum orbem suum ferendum per incrementa radiorum. sic ergo et Christus, id est imago dei et filius dei, ab hominibus inspicitur, qua poterat uideri. et ideo fragilitas et mediocritas sortis humanae per ipsum alitur, producitur, educatur, ut aliquando deum quoque ipsum patrem, assueta filium conspicere, possit, w est, uidere; ne maiestatis ipsius repentino et intolerabili fulgore percussa intercipi possit, ut deum patrem quem semper optauit uidere non possit. ex quo filius est hic qui uidetur; dei autem filius, dei uerbum est; dei autem uerbum caro factum est et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. quae, malum, ratio est ut dubitetur deus dici, qui tot modis deus intellegitur approbari? Ac si et Agar ancillam Sarae de domo eiectam pariter et fugatam angelus conuenit apud fontem aquae in uia Sur, fugae causas interrogat atque accipit, et post haec humilitatis consilia porrigit, spem praeterea illi materni nominis facit, quodque ex utero eius multum semen esset futurum spondet atque promittit, et quod Hismael ex illa nasci haberet, et cum ceteris aperit locum habitationis ipsius, actumque describit: hunc autem angelum et dominum scriptura proponit et deum (nam nec benedictionem seminis promisisset, nisi angelus et deus fuisset): quaerant quid in praesenti loco haeretici tractent. - pater fuit iste qui ab Agar uisus est, an non? quia deus positus sed absit deum patrem angelum dicere; ne alteri subsed angelum dicent fuisse. quomodo ergo deus erit, si angelus fuit, cum non sit hoc nomen angelis umquam concessum? nisi quoniam ex utroque latere nos ueritas in istam concludit sententiam, qua intellegere debeamus dei filium fuisse: qui, quoniam ex deo est, merito deus, quia dei filius, dictus sit, quoniam patri subditus et annuntiator paternae uoluntatis est, magni consilii angelus pronuntiatus est. ergo si hic locus neque personae patris congruit, ne angelus dictus sit, neque personae angeli, ne, deus pronuntiatus sit; personae autem Christi conuenit ut et deus sit, quia dei filius est, et angelus sit, quoniam paternae dispositionis annuntiator est: intellegere debent contra scripturas se agere haeretici, qui Christum cum dicant se et angelum credere, nolint illum etiam deum pronuntiare, quem in ueteri testamento ad uisitationem generis humani legunt\ saepe uenisse. Adhuc adiecit Moyses, Abrahae uisum deum apud quercum Mambre, sedente ipso ad ostium tabernaculi sui meridie, et nihilominus, cum tres conspexisset uiros, unum ex illis dominum nuncupasse; quorum cum pedes lauisset, cinericios panes cum butyro et ipsius copia lactis offert, et ut hospites retenti uescerentur, hortatur. post quae et quod pater futurus esset, audit; et quod Sara uxor eius paritura ex ipso filium esset, ediscit; et de exitu Sodomitarum, quae merebantur pati, recognoscit; et quod propter clamorem Sodomorum deus descendisset, addiscit. quo in loco si patrem uolunt uideri tunc fuisse cum angelis duobus hospitio receptum, patrem uisibilem haeretici crediderunt: si autem angelum, cum ex angelis tribus unus dominus nuncupatur, cur, quod non solet, angelus deus dicitur? nisi quoniam, ut deo patri inuisibilitas propria reddatur, et angelo propria mediocritas remittatur, non nisi dei filius, qui et deus est, Abrahae uisus et hospitio receptus esse credetur. quod enim erat futurus, meditabatur in sacramento Abrahae factus hospes, apud Abrahae filios futurus; cuius filiorum pedes, ad probationem quod ipse esset, abluit; reddens in filiis ius hospitalitatis, quod aliquando illi fenerauerat pater. unde et ne qua esset dubitatio quin iste Abrahae hospes fuisset, in Sodomitarum exitu ponitur: quoniam pluit dominus super Sodomam et Gomorram ignem et sulphur a domino de caelo. sic enim et prophetes ex persona dei: subuerti uos, inquit, sécut subuertit dominus Sodomam et Gomorram. dominus ergo Sodomam subuertit, id est, deus Sodomam subuertit: sed.in subuersione Sodomorum dominus pluit ignem a domino. hic autem dominus uisus est Abrahae deus: deus autem hic hospes est Abrahae uisus utique quia tactus. sed cum pater, quia inuisibilis, nec tunc utique uisus sit, uisus est et hospitio receptus et acceptus est, qui solitus est tangi et uideri: hic autem filius dei dominus a domino pluit super Sodomam et Gomorram sulphur atque ignem. hic autem dei uerbum est: uerbum autem dei caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis: hic autem Christus est. non pater igitur apud Abraham hospes, sed Christus fuit; nec tunc pater uisus est, sed filius; uisus autem est Christus. merito igitur Christus et dominus et deus est, qui non aliter Abrahae uisus est, nisi quia ante ipsum Abraham ex patre deo deus sermo generatus est. Adhuc, inquit, idem angelus et deus eandem Agar, fugatam de domo Abrahae cum puero, consolatur et uisitat. nam cum illa in solitudine exposuisset infantem, quia aqua defecisset ex utre, cumque puer ille clamasset, fletum et planctum leuasset, et audiuit, inquit scriptura, deus uocem pueri ae loco ubi erat. cum deum esse, qui uocem audisset infantis, rettulisset, adiecit: et uocauit angelus domini ipsam Agar de caelo; angelum referens esse quem deum dixerat, et~dominum pronuntians esse quem angelum collocarat.. quique angelus et deus adhuc ipsi Agar promittit maiora solacia, dicendo: ne timueris; exaudiui enim uocem pueri de loco ubi erat. surge, sume puerum, et tene: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum. hic angelus, si angelus tantum est, cur hoc sibi uindicat ut dicat: in gentem enim magnam faciam eum, cum hoc utique genus potentiae dei sit, angeli esse non possit? ex quo etiam deus confirmatur esse qui hoc potest facere. quoniam ut hoc ipsum comprobetur, adicitur per scripturam statim: e aperuit deus oculos eius, et uidit puteum aquae uiuae, et abiit, et impleuit utrem de puteo, et dedit puero, et erat deus cum puero. si ergo hic deus erat cum puero, qui aperuit oculos Agar, ut uideret puteum aquae uiuae et hauriret aquam propter urgentem sitis necessitatem; hic autem deus e caelo illam uocat; angelus dictus, cum superius uocem audiens clamantis pueri deus esset potius, non alius intellegitur quam angelus esse pariter et deus. quod cum patri competens et conueniens esse non possit, qui tantummodo deus est, competens autem esse possit Christo, qui non tantummodo deus sed et angelus pronuntiatus est, manifeste apparet non patrem ibi tunc locutum fuisse ad Agar, sed Christum potius, cum deus sit, cui etiam angeli competit nomen, quippe cum magni consili angelus factus sit; angelus autem sit, dum exponit sinum patris, sicut Ioannes edicit. si enim ipse Ioannes hunc eundem, qui sinum exponit patris, uerbum dicit carnem factum esse, ut sinum patris posset exponere, merito Christus non solum homo est, sed et angelus; nec angelus tantum, sed et deus per scripturas ostenditur, et a nobis hoc esse creditur, ne, si non Christum tunc locutum ad Agar uoluerimus accipere, aut angelum deum faciamus, aut deum patrem omnipotentem inter angelos computemus.
pass_a_gloss: Behold, Moses also reports in another place that God was seen by Abraham. That no man can see God and live. How can God be seen, since God cannot be seen? He says that no man has ever seen Him; no one can see Him. He is lying; therefore, God was truly seen. From this, it can be understood that it was not the Father who was seen, who has never been seen, but the Son, who is accustomed to descend and be seen because He descended. For the image of the invisible God is the Son, so that the weakness and fragility of human condition might gradually become accustomed to seeing God the Father in the image of God, that is, in the Son of God. For human weakness had to be nourished gradually through the image to this glory, so that it might be able to see God the Father someday, because great things are dangerous if they are sudden. For even the light of the sun, after darkness, does not show the day to unaccustomed eyes with too much splendor, but rather causes blindness. So that this might not happen to the detriment of human eyes, the rising of this light, gradually breaking through and dispelling the darkness, slowly accustoms human eyes to bear its entire orb through the increments of its rays. Thus, Christ, who is the image of God and the Son of God, is seen by men insofar as He can be seen. And therefore, the weakness and fragility of the human condition are nourished, produced, and educated through Him, so that someday, having become accustomed to seeing the Son, it might be able to see God the Father Himself; lest it be struck by the sudden and intolerable splendor of His majesty and be unable to see God the Father, whom it has always desired to see. From this, it is the Son who is seen; and the Son of God is the Word of God; and the Word of God became flesh and dwelled among us: this is Christ. What evil reasoning is it to doubt that He is called God, who is approved as God in so many ways? And if the angel met Hagar, the servant of Sarah, who was cast out of the house and fled, at the spring of water on the road to Shur, and asked her the reasons for her flight, and received them, and after these things gave her counsel of humility, and also gave her hope of the name of mother, and promised that there would be a great multitude of offspring from her, and that Ishmael would be born from her, and showed her the place of her habitation, and described her actions: let the heretics examine what is being discussed in this present passage. Was it the Father who was seen by Hagar, or not? Because God is mentioned, but it is absurd to call God the Father an angel; lest they say that another angel was present. How, then, can He be God if He was an angel, since this name has never been given to angels? Unless, indeed, the truth from both sides concludes us to this sentence, that we ought to understand it to be the Son of God: who, because He is from God, is rightly called God, because He is the Son of God; and because He is subject to the Father and the announcer of the Father's will, He is proclaimed to be the angel of great counsel. Therefore, if this passage does not fit the person of the Father, lest He be called an angel, nor the person of an angel, lest He be called God; but it does fit the person of Christ, that He is both God, because He is the Son of God, and an angel, because He is the announcer of the Father's disposition: the heretics ought to understand that they are acting against the Scriptures, who say that they believe Christ to be an angel, but do not want to proclaim Him to be God, whom they read to have come often to visit the human race in the Old Testament. Moreover, Moses added that God was seen by Abraham at the oak of Mamre, while Abraham was sitting at the door of his tent at noon, and nonetheless, when he saw three men, he called one of them Lord; and when he washed their feet, he offered them ashes and bread with butter, and an abundance of milk, and urged them to eat as guests. After these things, he heard that he would be a father; and he learned that his wife Sarah would bear a son from him; and he recognized the outcome of the Sodomites, who deserved to suffer; and he learned that God had descended because of the cry of the Sodomites. In this passage, if they want the Father to have been seen then with the two angels who were received as guests, the heretics have believed in a visible Father: but if it was an angel, since one of the three angels is called Lord, why is an angel called God, which is not usual? Unless, indeed, in order that the invisibility proper to God the Father might be preserved, and the mediocrity proper to an angel might be remitted, it is believed that the Son of God, who is also God, was seen by Abraham and received as a guest. For what was going to happen, He was meditating in the sacrament, having become a guest of Abraham, and would be among the sons of Abraham; whose feet, as a proof that He Himself was, He washed; rendering in the sons the right of hospitality, which the Father had once rendered to Him. Whence, also, so that there might be no doubt that this guest of Abraham was He, it is stated in the outcome of the Sodomites: for the Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord out of heaven. Thus, the prophet speaks in the person of God: 'I will overthrow you,' he says, 'as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.' Therefore, the Lord overthrew Sodom, that is, God overthrew Sodom: but in the overthrow of the Sodomites, the Lord rained fire from the Lord. This Lord, however, was seen by Abraham as God; and God is this guest who was seen by Abraham, certainly because He was touched. But since the Father, because He is invisible, was not seen then, He who is accustomed to be touched and seen was seen and received as a guest: this is the Son of God, the Lord, who rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord. This, however, is the Word of God: and the Word of God became flesh and dwelled among us: this is Christ. Therefore, it was not the Father who was the guest of Abraham, but Christ; and it was not the Father who was seen then, but the Son; and Christ was seen. Therefore, Christ is rightly Lord and God, who was seen by Abraham in no other way than because, before Abraham, the Word of God was generated from God the Father. Moreover, it is said that the same angel and God consoled and visited Hagar, who was cast out of Abraham's house with her son. For when she had exposed the infant in the wilderness, because the water had failed from the skin, and the boy had cried out, and she had raised her weeping and lamentation, and the Scripture says that God heard the voice of the boy from the place where he was. When it had been said that it was God who heard the voice of the infant, it was added: and the angel of the Lord called her, Hagar, from heaven; referring to the angel as the one whom He had called God, and proclaiming Him to be the Lord whom He had placed as an angel. And this angel and God promised greater solace to Hagar, saying: 'Do not fear; for I have heard the voice of the boy from the place where he was. Rise, take the boy, and hold him; for I will make him a great nation.' This angel, if he is only an angel, why does he claim for himself the right to say: 'I will make him a great nation,' since this is a kind of power that belongs to God, and cannot belong to an angel? From which it is also confirmed that He is God, who can do this. For in order to prove this very thing, it is added through Scripture: 'And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water, and she went and filled the skin from the well, and gave it to the boy, and God was with the boy.' If, then, this was God who was with the boy, who opened Hagar's eyes so that she might see the well of living water and draw water because of the urgent necessity of thirst; and this God called her from heaven; and the angel is called, since above it was said that God was hearing the voice of the crying boy, it is not understood to be another than the angel who is also God. Which, since it is fitting and suitable for the Son, who is not only God but also an angel, and not for the Father, who is only God, it clearly appears that it was not the Father who spoke to Hagar then, but rather Christ, who is God, to whom the name of angel is also suitable, since He has been made the angel of great counsel; and He is an angel, since He reveals the bosom of the Father, as John declares. For if John himself says that this same one, who reveals the bosom of the Father, is the Word who became flesh, so that He might reveal the bosom of the Father, it is right that Christ is not only man, but also an angel; and not only an angel, but also God, as is shown through the Scriptures, and is believed by us, lest, if we do not want to accept that Christ spoke to Hagar then, we either make an angel into God, or count God the Father among the angels.

pass_b_english: Moses also reports in another place that God was seen by Abraham. Since no human being can see God and live, how can God be seen when God cannot be seen? The objection runs: 'No man has ever seen Him; no one can see Him.' That is a lie; therefore God was truly seen. From this we can understand that it was not the Father who was seen — for the Father has never been seen — but the Son, who is accustomed to descend and to be seen precisely because He descended. For the Son is the image of the invisible God, so that the weakness and fragility of the human condition might gradually become accustomed to seeing God the Father in the image of God, that is, in the Son of God (Colossians 1:15; John 1:18). Human weakness had to be nourished step by step through that image toward this glory, so that it might someday be able to see God the Father; for great things are dangerous when they come suddenly. Even the light of the sun, bursting forth after darkness, does not show the day to unaccustomed eyes with its excessive splendor — it causes blindness instead. Lest this happen to the detriment of human eyes, the rising of this light, gradually breaking and dispelling the darkness, slowly accustoms human eyes to bear its entire orb through the increments of its rays. Thus Christ, who is the image of God and the Son of God, is seen by men insofar as He can be seen. And therefore the weakness and fragility of the human lot are nourished, brought forward, and educated through Him, so that someday, having grown accustomed to seeing the Son, they might be able to see God the Father Himself — lest they be struck down by the sudden and intolerable splendor of His majesty and fail to see the God the Father they have always longed to see (John 1:14). From this it follows that the Son is the one who is seen; and the Son of God is the Word of God; and the Word of God became flesh and dwelt among us: this is Christ (John 1:1, 14). What perverse reasoning leads anyone to doubt that He is called God, when He is shown to be God in so many ways?

Consider also Hagar, Sarah's servant, cast out and fleeing, whom the angel met at the spring on the road to Shur (Genesis 16:7-14). He questioned her about her flight, heard her answer, gave her counsel of humility, gave her hope of the name 'mother,' promised that her offspring would be multiplied, that Ishmael would be born to her, showed her a dwelling place, and foretold her future. Let the heretics examine what is at stake in this passage. Was it the Father who was seen by Hagar, or not? The text says 'God,' but it is absurd to call God the Father an angel — lest they claim a second angel was present. How then can He be God if He was an angel, since the name 'God' has never been granted to angels? Unless the truth from both sides forces us to the conclusion that this was the Son of God: who, because He is from God, is rightly called God, because He is the Son of God; and because He is subject to the Father and the announcer of the Father's will, He is proclaimed the angel of great counsel (Isaiah 9:6 LXX). Therefore, if this passage fits neither the person of the Father — lest He be called an angel — nor the person of an angel — lest he be called God — but fits the person of Christ, who is both God because He is the Son of God, and angel because He is the announcer of the Father's disposition, then the heretics must realize they are acting against the Scriptures. They say they believe Christ to be an angel, yet they refuse to proclaim Him God, whom they read in the Old Testament as having come often to visit the human race.

Moses adds that God was seen by Abraham at the oak of Mamre, while he sat at his tent door at noon (Genesis 18:1). When he saw three men, he called one of them Lord; he washed their feet and offered them bread with butter and milk in abundance, urging them to eat as guests. Afterward he heard that he would become a father, learned that Sarah would bear a son, recognized the coming doom of the Sodomites, and learned that God had descended because of the outcry against Sodom. In this passage, if the heretics want the Father to have been seen then together with two angels received as guests, they have believed in a visible Father. But if it was an angel, since one of the three is called Lord, why is an angel called God — which is not customary? Unless it is so that the invisibility proper to God the Father may be preserved, and the mediocrity proper to an angel may be set aside, and so that the Son of God, who is also God, is believed to have been seen by Abraham and received as a guest. For what was to come, He was foreshadowing in the sacrament by becoming Abraham's guest, destined to be among Abraham's sons; whose feet He washed as proof that He Himself was the one; rendering to the sons the right of hospitality which the Father had once entrusted to Him. And so that no doubt might remain that this guest of Abraham was He, the text records the destruction of the Sodomites: for the Lord rained fire and sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord out of heaven (Genesis 19:24). Thus the prophet speaks in God's person: 'I will overthrow you, as the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah' (Amos 4:11). Therefore the Lord overthrew Sodom — that is, God overthrew Sodom — but in the overthrow the Lord rained fire from the Lord. This Lord was the God seen by Abraham; and this God is the guest seen by Abraham, certainly because He was touched. But since the Father, being invisible, was certainly not seen then, the one who is accustomed to be touched and seen was seen and received as a guest: this is the Son of God, the Lord, who rained fire and sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord. This is the Word of God; and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us: this is Christ (John 1:14). Therefore it was not the Father who was Abraham's guest, but Christ; not the Father who was seen then, but the Son; and Christ was seen. Christ is therefore rightly Lord and God, who was seen by Abraham in no other way than because, before Abraham, the Word of God was begotten from God the Father (John 8:58).

Again, the same angel and God consoled and visited Hagar, cast out of Abraham's house with the boy (Genesis 16:7-14 continued). When she had left the infant in the wilderness because the water in the skin was gone, and the boy cried out, and she lifted up her weeping, Scripture says God heard the boy's voice from where he was (Genesis 16:17). When it had been stated that it was God who heard the infant's voice, it adds: 'And the angel of the Lord called to Hagar from heaven' (Genesis 16:17) — identifying the angel as the one just called God, and proclaiming Him Lord whom He had designated as angel. And this angel and God promised Hagar greater comfort: 'Do not fear; for I have heard the boy's voice from where he is. Rise, take the boy, and hold him; for I will make him a great nation' (Genesis 16:17-18). If this angel is only an angel, why does he claim the right to say, 'I will make him a great nation,' when this is a power belonging to God and cannot belong to an angel? From this it is also confirmed that He is God who can do this. To prove this very point, Scripture immediately adds: 'God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of living water, and went and filled the skin from the well, and gave it to the boy, and God was with the boy' (Genesis 16:19-20). If, then, this was God who was with the boy, who opened Hagar's eyes so she might see the well and draw water for the urgent need of thirst; and this God called her from heaven; and he is called angel, since above it was said that God heard the crying boy's voice — it is understood to be none other than the one who is both angel and God. Since this fits the Son, who is not only God but also angel, and not the Father, who is only God, it clearly appears that it was not the Father who spoke to Hagar then, but rather Christ, who is God, to whom the name of angel also belongs, since He has been made the angel of great counsel; and He is angel because He reveals the Father's bosom, as John declares (John 1:18). For if John himself says that this same one, who reveals the Father's bosom, is the Word made flesh, so that He might reveal the Father's bosom, then Christ is rightly not only man, but also angel; and not only angel, but also God, as shown through the Scriptures and believed by us — lest, if we refuse to accept that Christ spoke to Hagar then, we either make an angel into God, or count God the Father Almighty among the angels.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex Christological arguments regarding the visibility of the Son versus the invisibility of the Father. All scripture citations in Pass B (Colossians 1:15, John 1:18, John 1:14, Genesis 16:7-14, Isaiah 9:6, Genesis 18:1, Genesis 19:24, Amos 4:11, Genesis 16:17, Genesis 16:19-20, John 8:58) are correctly applied to the corresponding Latin/Greek concepts or allusions. The distinction between 'angelus' and 'deus' is maintained throughout. The title 'The Trinity and God's Visibility' correctly names the central thought of the chapter.
